To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the use of total pelvic exenteration (TPE) for locally advanced or recurrent rectal cancer is associated with a 5-year survival rate of approximately 50% and that TPE with preoperative radiation therapy (RT) is associated with a significantly higher 5-year survival and disease-free survival rates than is TPE with no preoperative RT.

1) total pelvic exenteration is feasible in patients with advanced primary and recurrent pelvic cancer; 2) preoperative irradiation can be administered safely; and 3) the results are comparable with those of other series of patients who have undergone similar operations.
the addition of preoperative irradiation to total pelvic exenteration for advanced primary or recurrent rectal cancer results in an improved survival and a lower local recurrence rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of preoperative radiation therapy (RT) on the surgical outcome and survival of patients with locally advanced primary and recurrent colorectal cancers.
the use of the total pelvic exenteration procedure for the treatment of locally advanced primary and recurrent cancer of the rectum.
the development of novel and innovative methods for the treatment of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of pelvic exenteration for recurrent rectal cancer in the absence of metastasis.

there is a role for preoperative radiation therapy and total pelvic exenteration for patients with advanced primary or recurrent rectal cancer who present with a tumor that is unresectable with conventional surgical techniques.
the use of a preoperative radiation therapy in combination with TME for patients with locally advanced rectal cancer does not improve survival.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, “The use of preoperative radiation therapy in the setting of total pelvic exenteration for locally advanced primary rectal cancer and recurrent rectal cancers is safe, effective, and associated with improved local control and overall survival.”

we can use the same model for the prediction of the outcome of patients with rectal cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiation and total mesorectal excision, regardless of the location of the primary tumor.
